newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Stormy debate over Hebron in Israeli cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Stormy debate over Hebron in Israeli cabinet.

text.p: Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu faced fierce opposition from right-wing ministers on Wednesday but his cabinet was expected to approve the Hebron withdrawal pact he sealed with the PLO.
Netanyahu's aides predicted the prime minister would secure a majority in the 18-member cabinet which met in stormy session for more than seven hours.
In Hebron, Israelis soldiers deployed to thwart Jewish settler protests and Palestinians put up welcome posters for President Yasser Arafat.
Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai ordered the army to wait until parliament approved the agreement on Thursday before handing most of the West Bank town over to Palestinians.
Parliament was expected to approve the deal with the support of the Labour and leftist party opposition. Security sources said redeployment would take less than 48 hours.
The United States hailed the accord that it brokered as a building block for Middle East peace.

Netanyahu and Arafat bowed to weeks of U.S. pressure and clinched the accord at an overnight summit. They also agreed Israel would complete three further pullbacks in the West Bank over the next 18 months.
U.S. mediators lit cigars like proud fathers after the tense talks at the Erez crossing between Israel and PLO-ruled Gaza.
But Arafat and Netanyahu did not seem overjoyed by the birth of an agreement that will give the PLO less land than it demanded and has caused a right-wing revolt in Israel's Likud-led coalition.
The two leaders were stern-faced. They briefly shook hands but did not speak to reporters. Palestinians said Netanyahu insisted the initialling of the accord be away from cameras.
The Hebron deal was an ideological wrench for Netanyahu and the Likud who had vowed never to cede part of the biblical Land of Israel to Palestinians.

Chief Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas told Reuters the deal requires Israel to withdraw from 80 percent of Hebron within 10 days and implement the first of three subsequent West Bank redeployments by March 7.
"It is the first agreement we have signed with the Likud. We hope this will be the beginning of more deals with this government," said Abbas, better known as Abu Mazen.

The peace process could run into trouble, however, over the scope of further withdrawals which Israeli officials say will give the Palestinians about only half the 90 percent of the West Bank they hope to control.
Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh told Israel Radio a U.S. letter of guarantees stated Israel would define the depth of the three additional West Bank pullbacks.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk confirmed the areas to be handed to the PLO in the three subsequent redeployments "is, according to the agreement, Israel's decision".

Israeli security sources said police and soldiers had been deployed in Hebron to prevent unrest ahead of the pullback from the town. Hebron, where some 400 militant Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Arabs, is a flashpoint of violence.
Hebronites put up posters to welcome Arafat although no one knew when he would arrive. Settlers cursed the accord and vowed to stay in the city.
U.S. mediator Dennis Ross said the agreement included a "note for the record" that dealt with the future Israeli redeployments from the West Bank and other non-Hebron related issues.

"These two documents represent a very important building block in terms of developing the relations between the two sides and in terms of laying out a pathway of greater hope and the possibility for peace in the Middle East," he said.

The Israeli opposition welcomed the agreement but blamed Netanyahu for damaging Israel's improving ties with the Arab world by holding up a Hebron deal just to make cosmetic changes for his right wing.
Asked how this Hebron accord differed from that signed by the ousted Labour government, former chief negotiator Uri Savir said: "Zero difference."

"It's basically the same agreement," he told Reuters. "The difference is in the atmosphere between us and the Palestinians...Unless the spirit of deep cooperation and dealing with the other side as equals returns, we might be in for a peace process lurching from crisis to crisis."
